Si una magnitud se calcula como $f(x, y,: If a quantity is calculated as $f(x, y, …)$ from measurements with uncertainties $Δx$, $Δy$…, each contributes its partial derivative times its uncertainty. If the errors are independent they add in quadrature; the linear bound (adding the absolute values) gives the worst possible case and is the one used in many lab manuals:
Para productos y cocientes de potencias,: For products and quotients of powers, $f = x^a y^b$, the relative errors are added: ${Δf}/{f} = √((a {Δx}/{x})^2 + (b {Δy}/{y})^2)$. That is why the measurement raised to a high power, like the period in $g = 4π^2 l/T^2$, is the one that weighs most.
La incertidumbre se da con <b>una cifra: The uncertainty is given with one significant figure, or two if the first is a 1 (0.014 and not 0.01). The value is rounded to the same decimal place as the uncertainty and they are written together with the unit: $g = (9.81 ± 0.05)$ m/s². Writing $9.810652 ± 0.05$ is a mistake: the last digits mean nothing.
Con n medidas de lo mismo se toma la med: With n measurements of the same thing the mean is taken. The spread is measured with the standard deviation $s$ (dividing by $n − 1$), and the mean differs from the true value by about $s/√n$, the standard error of the mean. It is combined in quadrature with the resolution of the instrument: if the instrument dominates, measuring more times improves nothing.
La suma en cuadratura solo vale si los e: Quadrature addition only holds if the errors are independent. If two variables rise and fall together (measured with the same badly calibrated instrument, or both coming from the same fit) a cross term with their covariance must be added, $"cov"(x, y) = r · Δx · Δy$, where $r$ is the correlation coefficient, between −1 and 1. The term carries the sign of the derivatives, so it can increase or reduce the error: in a sum with $r > 0$ the errors reinforce each other, and in a difference they cancel.
Cuando hay varias medidas de la misma ma: When there are several measurements of the same quantity with different uncertainties, they do not all weigh the same: each enters with weight $w_i = 1/σ_i^2$. The uncertainty of the mean is smaller than that of the best measurement. The reduced $χ^2$ tells whether the measurements are compatible with each other: close to 1, they are; if considerably larger, they differ more than their uncertainties say, and here the uncertainty of the mean is enlarged by multiplying it by $√{χ^2_"red"}$.
Para saber si un resultado concuerda con: To know whether a result agrees with the table value, the percentage difference is not enough: the discrepancy must be measured in uncertainties, $z = |x − x_"ac"|/√{Δx^2 + Δx_"ac"^2}$. Up to 1 σ the result is compatible; up to 2 σ, compatible at 2σ (it happens in one in three correct measurements); between 2 and 3 σ it is doubtful, and above 3 σ it is incompatible: there is a systematic error or the uncertainty is underestimated.
